subtopic: CONFERENCE
speechtext: am sure the house will have no objection to my saying that we are glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is back from his successful trip. I have a question I should like to ask him which it may be difficult to answer at this time. Perhaps he could take this by way of notice. Is the situation at the international wheat conference today such as would lead one to believe that a continuation of the agreement is not going to be achieved?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in close touch with the Canadian delegation at the conference. I must point out that the sessions are in private and no information is being given out in any form. My hon. friend will appreciate that I cannot give out any information from proceedings being held in camera. Meetings between importers and exporters are taking place each day.
I know of nothing that has happened that would lead to the conclusion that there is any breakdown in the discussions. Bargaining is going on and I am most hopeful, and I think most of those present at the conference are hopeful, that an agreement can be reached.
The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott that the house go into committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I had risen to speak at three minutes to ten but of course I had not got very far in what I was prepared to say. I rose at that time and I rise now to support the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) and the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) in their pleas on behalf of the sugar beet industry and the sugar refining industry in Canada. I was particularly interested in what they had to say, and I was also interested in the reply given by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). I should like 

to read a few extracts from the hon. member's speech and comment upon them as I go along. At the top of page 1819 of yesterday's Hansard the hon. member for Charlotte was explaining the economy of the maritime provinces in respect to the agreements that were made some time ago regarding the importation of Cuban sugar and the exportation of maritime fish. He said:
Again, I want to say that all the maritime provinces-and I will include Newfoundland because now we have four maritime provinces-as I have said on many occasions in this chamber, are most dependent on these American markets. Take them away from us and our economy is completely wrecked.
I believe I cam understand the mentality of the hon. member when he says:	"Take
them away from us and our economy is completely wrecked." In other words, the economy of the maritimes is completely dependent upon exports and imports, upon foreign trade. Might I ask the hon. member, and this is not the first time I have asked this question in this house:	What is the
purpose of an economic system? That question has never been answered by any member of the government. I would ask the government, I would ask the finance minister who is in charge of monetary policy, what is the purpose of an economic system? Until that is answered we are not going to solve our financial problems internally or externally.

You mean not until they are
"Hanselled".

We are not going to solve
the problem of foreign markets either. I am going to give hon. members my definition of the purpose of an economic system. I would suggest it is to produce and deliver for the welfare of man. I suggest that the monetary policy of any country should be designed to distribute the abundance that it is able to produce. That is the purpose of an economic system. The present government-in fact I would say all ox-cart economists-never admit that there is anything basically wrong with our present financial policy. They will never admit it. In fact everything that is done in the realm of finance is done for the purpose of bolstering, fortifying or solidifying, if you wish, the present financial policy, which is basically wrong. Everything that is done is done with that one purpose in mind regardless of how it affects the welfare of mankind.
In his speech the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) had a good deal to say with respect to free trade. When he mentioned free trade in the manner in which he did there was considerable applause from

the Liberal side of the house. Let me say that I think we are all in favour of as much free trade as possible. I believe we are all in favour of freer trade. But let me say that in the final analysis there is no such thing as free trade and there never will be. We may as well get ourselves straight on that. In spite of all the applauding that some members may do, there is no such thing as free trade. When I was a boy my father used to say that he was a Liberal. I do not know whether or not he was, but I know that I used to hear him talk about the Liberal party as being a free trade party. I heard a speaker in the house some year or two ago-I cannot recall who it was but what he said was not denied-who stated that during Liberal administration tariffs had on the average been higher than during Conservative administration.
Perfectly true, too.

That may or may not be so,
but with all the talk and applause that has come from the Liberal benches in respect of free trade-
Pure lip service.

-may I point out that they are in the driver's seat. The country is being administered by a Liberal administration, a so-called free-trade administration. Let them put some of their policies into action. I say that free trade is an absolute impossibility, and I would challenge any of them to name one thing that we can produce more cheaply in Canada than it can be produced in some other country. Let them name one thing that we can produce in Canada and sell in open competition with the world.
It would be a nice exercise.

That is a challenge. Let
them tell us.
What about nickel?

I was interested in reading an editorial in the Ottawa Journal the other day which is headed, "Wise Words from a Banker". It is not very often that Social Crediters quote bankers but bankers are at least authorities on banking. The president of such a well established bank as the Bank of Montreal certainly should know what he is talking about when he is dealing with economics. Of course even the president of the Bank of Montreal would not admit that there is something basically wrong with the present financial policy, and he is speaking of course as an orthodox banker and is analysing the present situation. Mr. B. C. Gardner, the able president of the Bank of
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement Montreal, made a speech, and the Ottawa Journal refers to it. This is what Mr. Gardner said:
Trade is in its nature competitive. Canada can ill afford, therefore, to come under the competitive disadvantage that we would suffer if our domestic level of prices should in future years rise more rapidly than corresponding prices in the United States. In a highly competitive world we cannot proceed on the assumption that domestic cost levels will be a matter of small moment as far as our export trade is concerned.
Further on there is the following:
Mr. Gardner concluded by pointing to other dangers-
Listen to this.
-a corporate tax rate which takes more than half of every dollar of profit, denying industry provision for necessary expansion; high taxation leading to compensatory wage demands and inviting inflation; public demands for government services which must be paid for out of the pockets of private citizens; a tendency to run to the government for protection against the ordinary hazards of day to day business. "There is great need for public education in these fields . . . for legislators and electorate alike."
That would include the hon. member for Charlotte. The fact of the matter is that, with our particular financial policy in Canada and its effect upon Canadian price levels, we cannot compete on world markets in the sale of practically anything. We cannot produce as cheaply as some other country in the world can produce. I want to read another extract from the speech of the hon. member for Charlotte. This is what he said, as found on the same page, page 1819 of Hansard of yesterday:
We do not get very many subsidies down there, and we do not get very much financial assistance. We are quite an understanding people, and we try to stand on our own feet. We are willing to produce what we have to produce in competition with any part of the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want hon. members to note that, because the actual truth is far, far beyond that statement.
We are willing to produce what we have to produce in competition with any part of the world. If we cannot produce fish as cheaply as someone else, then let us eat someone else's fish. If we cannot produce sugar as cheaply as we can buy it somewhere else then let us give the consumer the advantage of cheaper living.
That sounds all right, but let us analyse that statement and let me ask the hon. gentleman a question. He says:
We are willing to produce what we have to produce in competition with any part of the world. If we cannot produce fish as cheaply as someone else, then let us eat someone else's fish.
Will he then explain please why this government permits a 33 per cent tariff protection on codfish? Would he be willing to have that tariff taken off? Does he want it removed? Since he referred in another

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement part of his speech to the fact that potatoes are produced in the maritimes, does he believe that potatoes should not be protected- when at the present time there is a tariff of 75 cents per hundred pounds? We all recall what happened not so long ago when there was no market for potatoes grown in the maritimes. The dominion government bought the crop. What did they buy the crop for? They bought it to keep prices up. Is that not protection?
Now, the hon. member had better answer some of those very simple questions.
He says in another passage which I will quote from Hansard of yesterday:
I think we have to make it clear that if a business cannot stand on its own feet it should not exist. That might be a pretty broad statement, but if an industry cannot survive without subsidies, then there is something wrong.
Well, there certainly is something wrong, and it is not that there is something wrong with business. As a matter of fact business in Canada is run pretty efficiently. What is wrong can be found in some of the basic principles of our financial policies in Canada, and business must groove itself according to the financial policies which are determined by the present, government.
Let us get back to the subject of free trade and foreign markets to which my hon. friend referred, and we bring in the sugar beet industry. For a number of years now, particularly since the war, the nations-the United States, Canada and other countries -have been doing all they could-
Might I ask the hon. member a question?
Since I have been referring to the hon. gentleman's speech, yes.
Has the hon. member ever produced sugar beets, fish or anything else in his lifetime?
I did not get the first part of the question.
Has the hon. member ever produced sugar beets, agricultural products or fisheries products?
No, but he read a book.
"It's in the book".
I have not produced sugar beets except in my own backyard and I have never produced any fish except those I have caught with a hook, line and sinker.
Were they voters?
You want to try it because you might change your mind.
Order.
Mr. Speaker, in order for one to familiarize oneself with fish or sugar beets, it is not necessary for one to have grown them. I might ask my friend if he has ever preached a sermon in his life.
I think perhaps I have.
Well, that is very good.
His sermon has some sense to it.

That is what I am doing.

Mr. Speaker, I was saying
that we have done all we could during and since the war to rehabilitate war-torn countries. We have contributed to foreign aid. There is the Marshall plan, which has poured millions and millions of dollars into European countries. We have UNESCO, which was designed to educate people-to give them a scientific knowledge of production and other matters. We have the Colombo plan and we have had one thing after another.
Are you against them?

No, sir, I am not against
them. My hon. friend asks if I am against them. No, we are not; and I am making a point of why we do these things. Well, they were all designed to restore the productive capacities of war-torn countries. What for? You might say that is a foolish question; but the answer is: So that they can produce; so that they can become self-sufficient. That is the answer.
It is a simple answer.

Just as simple as that. But
let us remember that the more that nations become self-sufficient the less they become dependent on foreign trade.
No, no.

Well, unless we are going to manufacture wheelbarrows and exchange them for wheelbarrows from some other country-and surely we do not adjust our economies to do that.
Let me read a little excerpt from the Pakistan News and Views of February 2. It is a very interesting item regarding a
>
speech that was given by Mr. Nurul Amin, chief minister of East Pakistan. I will read it:
Land which formerly produced jute is now going to be used to grow more food for the populous area of East Pakistan. The chief minister of East Pakistan, Mr. Nurul Amin, has expressed the hope that this will enable East Pakistan to wipe out its food deficit in two years.
They are going to become self-sufficient in respect of their production of foods in two years. I will not take time to read the whole article but the final paragraph reads:
In conclusion, the chief minister stated that selfsufficiency in food was the first objective of every country. "But", he added, "it is more so in the case of East Pakistan which has an enormous population."
Now, Mr. Speaker, one might say that to take such an attitude is to lean toward nationalism. Well, if that is so in contradistinction to the position of the internationalists, then I do not mind being called a nationalist. Furthermore, if we are to be accused of attempting to safeguard our sovereignty, I do not mind being accused of that either. To add it up and conclude, all you are accusing one of is simply being a Canadian. You can accuse us of that if you wish. You can say that we are ultra-Canadian if you wish. I say that we believe in foreign trade. We believe also in using our productive capacity to produce Canadian goods for Canadian people. What we say is simply this. We can produce sugar in Canada, and there is no reason why we should not produce sugar for Canadian consumption.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a brief that has been published by the Alberta sugar beet growers. I am not going to read the entire brief, but I am going to read that part of it which sums up one or two of the reasons for the continuation and expansion of the sugar industry in Canada for Canadians. I read this from the brief:
Several policies of the Canadian government are directly affected by the potential influx of foreign refined sugars into Canada.
Then, the brief gives some of the reasons for the necessity of sugar production in this country. The first one in the brief, numbered "A", is as follows:
The defence policy-which makes it vital to Canada, that a reasonable proportion of this country's sugar supply be produced at home. The lesson of sugar rationing and shortages during the last war should be remembered. During that period of stringency-due to submarine sinking of sugar ships-it was required that Alberta sugar be shipped to Ontario and Quebec.
We do not have to comment on that. We all know that sugar is a vital food product in Canada. The nation could not live without sugar, and yet as soon as the last war 08108-117
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement broke out one of the first things to be rationed was sugar. I am quite certain in my own mind that the reason for that was the lack of foresight on the part of the administration here to ensure that there were ample supplies of sugar in Canada. The sugar industry should have been encouraged to produce more for Canadian consumption. We were running around with saccharine tablets in our pockets to put in our tea and coffee. When the fruit season came along and the housewives desired to preserve fruit, what happened? They were allowed a few extra coupons in order to put by some preserves for the winter. This state of affairs really should not have occurred in Canada, yet it did. I say once again that this portion of the brief represents one reason why we should pay attention to the sugar industry of Canada, if for no other reason, because it ties in with an adequate defence policy.
Another reason given in the brief is that the industry helps in our immigration policy. I will read from the brief:
The immigration policy, which calls for the establishment of agricultural people on the Canadian farm lands-as these people from Europe come to a sugar beet area, they are able to establish themselves first as beet labourers, then as tenant farmers, then owners of farms themselves. This process has gone on continually in southern Alberta and many of our best irrigation farmers are those who entered the sugar beet industry as hand labourers.
I am told that about 10,000 people have been brought into these areas. Well, I shall read that portion of the brief.
Since the opening of immigration-post-war, we estimate over 1,000 people each year have been so employed. In seven years, this immigration has amounted to around 10,000 people who are building up Canada. The present population of 100,000 people in the area surrounding Lethbridge, our market town centre, is very largely composed of immigrants attracted by the sugar beet industry.
Then, another reason for supporting the sugar industry in Canada is the irrigation policy. I shall read this short paragraph from the brief:
The irrigation policy. Millions of dollars from governments in Canada have been and are being spent to place water on arid and semi-arid lands. We state, without fear of challenge, that sugar beets as a cash crop, are the foundation for the successful farming, which must follow irrigation in western Canada. The introduction of rotation, use of beet by-products, for supplementing grasses and legumes, the establishment of livestock farming, all rely upon sugar beets.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could read more from that brief and comment further upon it but I do not wish to detain the house. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has given a great deal of study during the past twenty years to the sugar industry of Canada, and he will have something to say upon this
1335	HOUSE OF
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement matter. I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that on the subject of _ the sugar industry the member for Lethbridge is an expert. It would pay this house to listen to what he has to say in this connection. It is of vital importance to Canada. We are not simply making claims for the industry itself, we are making claims on behalf of the Canadian nation. We believe that the policy of producing Canadian goods for Canadian people is the right policy. Since sugar is a vital food product, we believe in the production of Canadian sugar for Canadian consumption.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I greatly
appreciate the warmth of the welcome that I have received upon returning to the House of Commons. Last evening I returned from a trip that covered 20,000 miles of travel by air, and which included visits to eleven different countries. I hope in due course to be able to give a report to the house of some of the highlights of the trip, perhaps on the estimates of the department. At the moment, I should like to speak about sugar.
I was not able to do so earlier. Perhaps hon. members would be interested in my contact with this problem.
Some time early in last October I had a call from Mr. McGregor of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company, pointing out that imports of Cuban refined sugar were coming into western Ontario and disturbing the market for beet sugar. At that time he asked that a quota be placed on imports of refined sugar into Canada. I pointed out that quantitative restrictions were one of the menaces to world trade today and that Canada was vigorously protesting quantitative restrictions against the importation of Canadian cheese into the United States market and against other similar violations of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. He was not satisfied with that, but he departed. A few days later I was asked to meet a group of beet sugar growers and refiners, which I did. Quite a large group came to Ottawa. Representatives of the industry in Alberta, in Manitoba, in western Ontario and in Quebec came here. We had a frank discussion. Several facts emerged from it. One fact that was stated repeatedly was that the agreement with Cuba covering the import of raw sugar had no bearing on the problem whatever. That was stated several times by several members of the delegation and I thought it was accepted as a fact by all those present. Of course, it is a fact because the source of the raw sugar is immaterial if the laid-down price in Canada is the same from any country of
(Mr. Hansell.l

origin as it is in this case. The meeting was in agreement-I must say that the representative of the Quebec industry did not agree-that the whole difficulty was caused by the importation of refined sugar from Cuba. The representative from Quebec said that there were several things wrong with the industry, but the rest agreed absolutely that if the import of the refined sugar from Cuba could be stopped, the beet industry could carry on.
I promised the meeting that I would visit Cuba early in February-I had already planned to do that as part of my itinerary- and that I would take up with Cuban exporters the matter of stopping the import of Cuban refined sugar into the beet-growing areas. That was an undertaking, and both they and I understood that it was a binding agreement that I would do just that.
A short time after that the beet-growing industry was circularized by Mr. McGregor of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company, Limited and was asked to take part in a pressure campaign on the government to bring about legislation to stop the import of Cuban refined sugar. I am happy to say that the rest of the industry, being men of integrity, refused to have anything to do with that campaign and I was advised by them to that effect. However, the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company then started the most aggressive pressure campaign that I have ever known of ini my seventeen years as a member of this House of Commons. I have here cables that I received while on the trip; they include cables to Bogota, to Havana, to Rio and to other stopping places. They are all in the same language though not in the same words. It happens that Mr. McGregor is a man with a limited vocabulary and he repeats certain phrases. Those phrases are in all the cables. In the meantime the office received telegrams and letters obviously all written by Mr. McGregor or his staff and signed by parish priests, by organizations of growers, by individuals and by various other people, if there are any others.
The hon. member for Lambton West (Mr Murphy) undertook to take up the subject in the House of Commons and he did so. I presume that the hon. member for Lambton West prepared his own speech but I notice that the same old phrases that appeared in these letters and telegrams turned up frequently in his speech. It may be asked: Why did I not answer on this matter before I left? Would it not seem logical that I should do so when members from this side of the house spoke on this subject? I did not do so. The reason I did not was the commitment I had made to go to Cuba and

to take this matter up on the ground. I know from experience-as I think most other people do-that anything that is written on the subject of sugar in Canada or any speech made in the House of Commons on sugar is reprinted in full in Spanish in the Cuban newspapers. If I was going to talk to the Cuban industry, obviously I should not talk in Canada in this House of Commons; I should talk to them in Cuba. Therefore I made no reply to the speeches.
When I met with our beet growers at the end of October, I stated that I was reasonably sure that, if our position was laid before the Cuban authorities, the import of refined sugar would stop. I pointed out that the interest of Cuba was centred more on shipping raw sugar to Canada than on shipping refined sugar. I stated that I would find out how that refined sugar was coming in and would arrange to stop the import.
I arrived in Cuba. I found the industry greatly disturbed. They had been reading the speeches of the hon. member for Lambton West and they wanted to know whether Canada wanted to break trade relations with Cuba. I explained that the hon. member for Lambton West was simply a politician looking for the votes of the sugar growers and that they were not to take his remarks seriously.
However, we had thorough discussions. At a meeting attended by the principal exporters of the island I explained that we were glad to have their raw sugar but that their refined sugar was presenting a serious economic problem in Canada. They agreed at once that they had no desire to upset the Canadian economy and that if refined sugar was doing that, they would stop exporting it to the beet areas.
I then met the sugar institute, the body that controls all matters affecting sugar in the island of Cuba. I explained the situation to them. They very reasonably said:	"You
have a duty on refined sugar of $1.89 per 100 lbs., which is a duty of more than 25 per cent at present prices; if our sugar can come in over that duty, your refiners are getting too much profit." I said: "I know that; but nevertheless I am talking for the beet-sugar industry. Even though our cane refiners are taking too much profit, I want you to stop the shipment of refined sugar into the beet-growing areas." They pointed out some exceedingly bad buying practices on the part of our trade-practices which should be corrected. I am meeting our refiners at the end of the week and I hope that those buying practices can be corrected.

Is Mr. McGregor coming up?
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will be glad to talk to Mr. McGregor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Assuming that remedial action is taken with regard to these buying practices which have discriminated definitely against the Cuban exporters, I think I can assure hon. members that no Cuban refined sugar will be shipped from Cuba into western Ontario or into the three prairie provinces. It may be that if the refiners are still considered to be taking too wide a margin, refined sugar will go to Newfoundland, which was always a market for Cuban refined sugar, it may go into the maritime provinces. All I am saying is that refined sugar will" not be shipped directly from Cuba into the beet-growing markets.
I should like to say a little bit about Mr. McGregor's company. While we are going into this matter I think perhaps we had just better see what the real situation is. We must examine separately the interests of the refining company in question and those of the beet-sugar growers themselves; for, although some of the growers have allowed themselves to be persuaded to join in the representations of the refiners, it does not necessarily follow that their interests are identical.
let me say a few words about the position of this refining company. While I shall have to speak frankly in this connection, I should not like anyone to feel that this is being done in an unfriendly or critical spirit. The company in question is a reputable concern of many years' standing, respected in the community. Its affairs, so far as I know, are efficiently conducted, and if its recommendations are designed to benefit primarily the company itself this is not surprising nor anything with which one should necessarily find fault. The Canada and Dominion Sugar Company is the owner of three large refineries, two in western Ontario and one in Montreal. These refineries, according to figures recently published-and I quote from the Financial Post corporation service-have been doing approximately one-third of all the sugar refining business in Canada.
While the company processes beets in western Ontario, its principal activity is the refining of imported raw cane sugar. In the latest year for which I have seen statistics, for every pound of beet sugar produced by this company it was refining approximately four pounds of imported cane sugar.
During a number of years past, the company has been enjoying a period of quite profitable operations. Between 1945 and
1838	HOUSE OF
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement 1951 its net profits, after taxes, steadily rose from $940,638 in 1945 to $2,238,888 in 1950, an exceptionally good year-
The poor fellows!

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
-followed by a profit of $1,779,337 in 1951. Although I have not seen it authenticated, I am told that the gross profits of the company before write-off in 1952 were the highest in the history of the company. I would point out however that that prosperity in 1952 was not shared by the beet growers, who took a cut in their returns. I am afraid this refining company has not learned about equality of sacrifice.
Good dividends have been regularly paid for many years, and since the war the company has also managed to double its earned surplus which, at the end of 1951, amounted to more than $5 million. It is obvious that the main financial interest of this company lies in the refining of cane sugar, constituting about 80 per cent of its total output, with beet sugar as a profitable sideline.
The year 1950 was a record year for the sugar beet industry in Canada. In that year, from figures reported by the company itself, the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company produced about 494 million pounds of refined sugar, of which 104 million pounds were from beets and 390 million pounds from cane. To express the implications of these facts in more definite terms, if parliament should see fit to take some action which would have the effect of increasing the price of refined sugar in Canada by one cent a pound, this company would be placed in a position to collect from Canadian consumers, in round figures, an pxtra $5 million a year. Of this amount, about $1 million would go for beet sugar. And under the sliding scale of prices provided in the company's contracts, I understand that the beet growers would get about one-half of this sum, the company retaining the balance. Also, the whole of the $4 million arising from the increase in the price of refined cane sugar would be available to increase the profits of the company. I think I can understand why this company might have come to the conclusion that it would be a good thing to keep up the price of refined sugar in Canada, and to prevent the importation of competitive products or, what amounts to much the same thing, to restrict the imports to something less than 1 per cent of total Canadian consumption.
But I cannot quite see why the beet growers should be prepared to support this easy solution to their problems. Relatively speaking, they would get a very small share of the proceeds. In total, out of every additional dollar contributed by Canadian


sugar consumers, the beet growers would apparently stand to gain about 10 cents; the remainder would go to the refiners.
At this point it would be helpful to look at the magnitude of this problem. For the past four years our total imports of all raw and refined sugar into Canada averaged 600,000 short tons per year. Most imports of sugar into Canada are made by the refiners themselves. However, for many years we have been importing modest quantities of refined and other sugar for direct industrial use. Total imports of refined sugar for direct industrial use since the end of world war II have ranged from 4 to 13 thousand tons a year, and for 1952 may have reached 25,000 tons-less than 4 per cent of the total consumption of refined sugar in Canada. The solution proposed by the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company Limited and the beet sugar growers who are supporting them is a maximum import quota of 5,000 tons of refined sugar per year.
Once we adopted the policy of using import quotas as a permanent protective device for the benefit of the sugar refiners, does anybody imagine that other interests would be slow to appeal for a similar kind of protection? And how would the farmers of Canada like it if this parliament were to place virtually prohibitive import quotas on the things that they have to buy, wherever these articles happen to compete with goods produced in Canada? How would the exporters of Canada like it if their customers in other countries, not content with tariffs, were likewise to adopt import quotas to keep out Canadian products whenever these Canadian products showed signs of competing with their own industry? In instances where other governments have resorted to such policies, we have made vigorous protests. We should not expect our protests to be very effective, however, if we ourselves accepted the principle of virtually prohibitive import quotas as a part of the regular commercial policy of this country. There are very few countries which depend as much as Canada on
183S

two-way international trade, and it would not be logical for us, of all people, to set a bad example by adopting that kind of import restriction.
And now let me say a few words about the beet growing industry. This industry over the years has also grown and prospered. After the first great war the area under sugar beets in Canada ranged from 15 to 25 thousand acres. The value of the beets grown in Canada at that time was less than $2 million a year, and in 1922 beet sugar accounted for only 2-6 per cent of the total production of refined sugar in Canada. Since then, the beet growers have come a long way under our present sugar tariff structure. The number of acres in sugar beet has steadily increased to an all-time high of 101,650 acres in 1950, and nearly as much, 93,138 acres, in 1951. The total value of sugar beets grown in Canada reached an alltime high of $18,459,000 in 1950, as a result of good weather and abnormal raw cane sugar prices. The value of $14,364,000 in 1951 was the second highest in history. Beet sugar represented 19-6 per cent of the total Canadian production of refined sugar in 1950 and 18-9 per cent of the total in 1951. Hon. members will find an inspiring story of this industry in an article by George A. Yackulic in Saturday Night of February 7. In this article, headed "Hope and Fortune Found in Sugar Beets", the writer described the beet sugar industry in Alberta as having been a steppingstone to farm ownership for many hundreds of new Canadians. The writer reports that, by the time they finish collecting for their 1952 crop next fall, many of Alberta's farmers will count their profits from beets at over $100 per acre.
There is, of course, a difference between growing beets in Alberta and growing them in Ontario. The irrigated land of Alberta which is suitable for beet culture is far away from Canadian ocean ports. The beet growers of Alberta and to a lesser extent those of Manitoba, therefore, enjoy a natural freight protection against the competition of imported sugar. This may be illustrated by the following table of relative retail prices of refined sugar in eight Canadian cities on September 2 last:

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement therefore, more than sufficient to protect the production in western Canada, which benefits by freight protection in addition. In Ontario, recent figures indicate that the production of beet sugar is running at approximately 47,000 tons a year, about 7 per cent of the total production of refined sugar in Canada. In Ontario there are competitive demands for labour, notably in Windsor and Chatham; there are also competitive uses for land such as the production of soya beans and corn; but it is remarkable to see the way in which the sugar beet farmers of Ontario have continued to find it profitable in recent years to grow this crop.
We have heard a great deal in this house about the 6,000 sugar beet farmers in Ontario. According to the census of 1951, sugar beets were being grown during that year on 3,087 farms in Ontario on an area of 30,068 acres, being an average of 9.07 acres per farm. In Alberta and Manitoba, the operations were on a larger scale, the average area under sugar beets per farm in Alberta being 26.8 acres and in Manitoba 20.2 acres. In the province of Quebec, on the other hand, sugar beets were being grown on 2,494 farms on an area of 10,741 acres, being an average of 4.3 acres per farm.
The cause of the present complaints lies in the recent fall in world raw sugar prices, not in this small importation of Cuban refined sugar. What has brought this about? There is no mystery about it. During and after the second world war there was a temporary shortage of sugar, and prices went up. By the spring of 1950 production had increased and the price of raw sugar had fallen to about $4 per 100 lbs., f.a.s. Cuba.
The panic buying following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea pushed this price up to a high of better than $8 per 100 lbs., in July, 1951. Since that date production has been overtaking consumption, and within the last few months the supply of sugar available has increased to such a level that producing countries are holding substantial tonnages of raw sugar and the price has fallen as low as $3.50 per 100 lbs., f.a.s. Cuba, Neither the beet growers, for whom I have the greatest respect and sympathy, nor any other class of producers can hope to continue to receive at all times the full benefit of scarcity prices. For many years they enjoyed an extensive and profitable business at normal prices. During the last few years they have done even better. At the present time world sugar prices have returned to more normal levels.
There may be farmers who will find it more profitable to shift a part of their production into some other crop. Such shifts

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement happen every year. On the other hand, I have no doubt that even without any extraordinary measures to promote the growing of this crop, sugar beets will continue to be profitably grown in Canada as they have been throughout the past fifty years.
I appreciate the fact that the Canadian refiners have special problems of their own. Because of the seasonal nature of Canadian navigation they have to stock up for the winter and hold a considerable inventory which may rise or fall in value while they are holding it. In recent years raw sugar prices have been rising and I presume that refiners have taken a corresponding benefit. More recently, prices have been falling and it is evident that the refiners have naturally been postponing as long as possible the moment for making corresponding reductions in the prices of refined sugar. This is why industrial users of refined sugar in Canada have found it worth their while to import refined sugar from Cuba, even over a duty of nearly two cents a pound.
There is no doubt in my mind that it would be possible, if we thought it to Canada's advantage, to devise some kind of restrictions which would curtail or entirely prevent the importation of refined sugar from any source, though naturally the people of Canada would have to pay for it in higher prices, the loss of export markets, and retaliation in other countries.
In Cuba our export interests include fish, potatoes, wheat, and a very wide variety of manufactured products which the Cubans themselves would like to buy from us in larger quantities. A good many of these products come from Ontario and western Canada, the very provinces where sugar beets are grown.
It would surely be irrational to endanger our export markets for fish, potatoes and wheat and manufactured products and at the same time to increase the cost of living and the cost of production throughout Canada in order to safeguard one industry against all possible competition.
It is not the policy of this government or of the party to which I belong to respond to pressure organized and generated by a single company, even if it is the producer of one-third of all the refined sugar consumed in Canada.
A good deal has been said in this debate, particularly by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), who told us a very sad tale about the low wages paid in Cuba. I took particular pains to find out about wages in Cuba. The sugar producers have a


contract with the workers which is supervised by the government. I was able to get a document from the government in Spanish which gave the full particulars. I think Canadian sugar growers, who have been doing so well according to Mr. McGregor and the hon. member for Lambton West, might want to know what similar labour in Cuba is getting. They might revise their whole idea about returns for growing of sugar beets in western Ontario.
During my visit to Cuba a few days ago I obtained a substantial file of information with regard to wage rates paid to workers in the sugar industry and applicable to the 1953 sugar crop. I also obtained comparable information with regard to the 1950 crop. These wages are not by any means low.
Out of scores of occupations listed, I may quote a few typical ones. The lowest unskilled wage listed in the entire contract is the one for collectors of sugar samples, warehousemen, et cetera, who are getting $4.43 a day. Generally speaking, the wages for unskilled workers in the sugar mills range between $5 and $6 a day; the wages for more skilled workers range from $6 to $9 per day; and when we get into the classes of tradesmen the wages run from $9 to $15 a day. Foremen are getting $15 to $22 a day. It should be noted that all workers in Cuban sugar factories receive compulsory vacation pay as well as a number of extra benefits for retirement, maternity, et cetera. They operate on a 44-hour week. That is the answer to the sad story about the depressed wages paid to the poor coloured workers in the Cuban sugar industry.
I should like to quote from the Chatham Daily News of November 7, 1952, as follows:
For the second time within a quarter of a century the sugar beet industry in Ontario faces possible extinction as the Liberal government at Ottawa allows refined Cuban sugar to flood the domestic market. Noting that the price of beet sugar has dropped $10.80 to $8.60 within a sixteen month period and $1.30 since Cuba started flooding the market last February, beet processors admitted today that they are "stymied" in the face of government apathy.
I can tell you how beet sugar can be compensated if the price of refined sugar has only dropped to the extent indicated there while the price of raw cane sugar has dropped by $4.40. The beet sugar growers might ask the refiners for a little share of the extra gravy that is being withheld at the expense of the Canadian consumer.
I have some additional notes here. I had planned to really do a job on my friend, Mr. McGregor, in return for the loss of sleep he caused me on my trip, but I do not think I will say much more. One threat he made did not cause me very much concern. I have

heard it made before. It was a threat that unless Cuban refined sugar was shut out of Canada he would close the refineries. I would assume that Mr. McGregor has shareholders and a board of directors, and that just about the time he would start closing the refineries the board of directors would decide to get themselves a new head boy.
This has been a difficult negotiation. Our balance of trade with Cuba is very much in our favour, and Cuba is a very important market to the maritime provinces. It always has been and it always will be. The Cuban agreement on raw sugar was made as ' a means of stimulating that market and of protecting the market we have had. It has had that effect. There has been a very sharp growth in imports from the maritime provinces, and in talking to the people of Cuba I may say that they in Cuba believe that market can be stimulated a great deal more.
It was necessary to conduct these negotiations with that thought in mindu Certainly I have no intention at any cost of disturbing that market for products of the maritime provinces. However, it has been my experience that international traders are reasonable people and that they particularly value the good will of governments. I did not have much doubt when I went to Cuba that if this situation was explained to the exporters they would be prepared to co-operate. I found that to be the case, and I sincerely hope that nothing will be said in this house or outside of it that will further disturb the happy relations that exist between Canada and Cuba in the matter of raw and refined sugar and in the matter of interchange of products generally between our two countries.

I should like to ask the minister a question. I would be interested to know whether, if the importation of refined sugar from Cuba was prohibited, that would increase the cost of refined sugar to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: All I can say is, it would put the refineries in the position of being able to charge anything they like for refined sugar, and while I have great respect for the industry as a whole I have no respect at all for the president of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company. I shudder to think what he would do to our consumer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question? Can he explain why it is that the retail price of sugar at Winnipeg is so high, the second highest in the country of the list that he gave, in view of the fact that we have a refinery right at our back door?
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The prices of all products are based on competition. I presume it costs more to grow sugar beets in Manitoba than it does in Ontario. I do not believe that the beet sugar growers on the prairies could live on the price at which raw sugar can be landed at Canadian ports and refined there. The protection of course is the rail rate from the coast to the interior. I think the prices are just what one would expect, having in mind the cost of transporting imported sugar to the prairies.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who is getting the benefit of that freight rate protection, the growers or the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

Notwithstanding all that, however, I rise to voice a grievance. In my constituency, and in other beet sugar producing areas of Canada, there is definite injury by reason of the importation of Cuban refined. There is no objection to the importation of Cuban raw sugar, but when Cuban refined comes in we begin to remember the years 1930, 1931, 1929, 1928 and 1927, that period right up to 1932 when the Conservative government had to impose a minimum price of $2.30 a hundred at point of origin in order to save the beet sugar industry at all. We remember the fact that for some unaccountable reason the Liberal government at Ottawa abolished that provision in 1939, a provision which was the sole protection the beet sugar industry of Canada had against the importation of refined sugar from cane producing areas. They never told the country they did that. They did not get permission from parliament to do it. They did not even announce it. They just did it. Thereby the beet sugar growers were left completely at the mercy of cane producing areas where they could refine the raw cane into refined. That is the thing that is worrying us.
We can remember all the abominations committed against the beet sugar industry by the sugar controller during world war II. One of these days I will talk about them, and I believe they will be quite astounding to our maritime friends, for whom I have nothing but the very greatest sympathy.
You are always astounding.

I hope I always will be.
1 think it would do my hon. friend a lot of good to be astounded occasionally.
So, Mr. Speaker, we still think we have been injured and are in danger of being much more severely injured by the importation of Cuban refined sugar. We look upon the federal government's neglect to limit the importation of this Cuban refined sugar into Canada as a neglect of duty.
I propose to show the vital importance of the beet sugar industry in the Canadian economy with respect to several considerations.

Any nation that intends ever to be strong and enduring must have constantly in mind five essentials respecting its economy. The first is to keep enough of its youth and its immigrants at home to provide amply for its people-producers, consumers and defenders. The second is to keep enough of its money at home to avoid falling into debt abroad. The third is to keep farmers and other primary producers within its borders able to buy the output of the cities. The fourth is to keep its national plant from running down, in other words to husband its resources, managing as far as possible always to improve them and not to deplete them. The fifth is to keep its production stable by avoiding lopsidedness or development in one or two or a few crops, an economy resembling that of Cuba. To attain those five imperative national objectives, the beet sugar industry is the best means available to Canada-this is a matter of exceedingly serious importance, a thing altogether too much neglected.
The beet sugar industry is no longer an experiment. It has been long tried, long proven and long trusted. Germany and Russia and other continental European countries have proved it. Britain has proved, and so has the United States. Canada has proved it abundantly and beyond all possibility of doubt. By that I mean to say that the sugar beet industry is not on trial. The only ones on trial in this country are people who do not know about it. Canada has proved the beet sugar industry in respect of each of the five considerations I have mentioned.
Back in 1932, in the darkest of the depression years, it was estimated in the United States that a beet sugar factory of 1,200 tons slicing capacity would give a living directly and indirectly to 10,000 people. The factory at Raymond, Alberta, in my constituency, is of 1,200 tons slicing capacity and produces yearly about 45 million pounds of refined sugar. It employed 350 people in the factory, 2,200 workers in the fields and 700 growers. That factory used coal to the value of $55,000; lime rock to the value of $20,000; coke to the value of $9,000; boxes, supplies and maintenance to the value of $105,000; bags to the value of $100,000; freight rates to the value of $330,000. The factory payroll was $175,000, and it paid the growers $940,000.
From the standpoint of providing work and markets I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is not an industry in the Dominion of Canada or on the North American continent that can begin to compare with the beet sugar industry. Let it be borne in mind that if troubles come upon this nation tending toward depression the first thing we shall be
IMr. Blackmore.]

wanting will be jobs and markets. If we destroy this means of providing markets we will rue the day. Let us be wise enough not to be foolish in respect of the beet sugar industry.
This factory helped to keep busy the rail-waymen, miners, labourers, truckers and others. The proof of these figures will be found in "Why Canada needs sugar beets", pages 14 to 16.
In the Lethbridge area now there are three fine sugar factories at Raymond, Picture Butte and Taber. That will indicate the reason Lethbridge had a higher per capita income in 1952 than any other city or community in Canada. The Lethbridge district receives very little income from oil. There are hardly any oil wells there. All the prosperity which prevails in Alberta generally in respect of oil is not shared directly by Lethbridge.
Turning back to the Raymond factory, certainly from 1932 until now it ha9 kept a good many Alberta youths at home who otherwise would have gone to the United States. It thereby complies with the first national requirement. It has kept in Canada money that would otherwise have gone to Cuba or other dollar countries to pay for scores of millions of pounds of sugar. It has kept many farmers and others in a position where they have been able to buy manufactured goods from Ontario, Quebec and other parts of Canada. By reason of the manure from stockfeeding, of the fibers and nitrogen restored to the soil, through crop rotation it has helped to keep the soil in southern Alberta from running down. Finally, it has greatly diversified Alberta and Canadian farming, which is a matter of extreme importance. Every acre of properly managed Alberta sugar beet land takes ten acres out of production of wheat in Alberta. That results from the fact that one of a considerable number of crop rotations is used in making the land ready for each beet crop.
The Canadian farming industry is now specializing far too much in wheat growing. Through raising wheat and other grains we are mining our soil. May I repeat that we are mining the soil of Canada. The amount of nitrogen taken out of the soil in raising one bushel of wheat is 1-3 pounds. For oats the figure is -65 pounds; for barley -9 pounds. Now, imagine how much of the actual substance of Canadian soil we are sending out of this country when we ship 100 million bushels of wheat. That goes on every year, not just 100 million but 300 million and 350 million bushels.

What are you going to do about it?

Many of those who oppose, or adopt a lukewarm attitude to, the beet sugar industry argue that Canada should work for less restrictive trade, and toward free trade. For a moment may we examine this matter of freer trade, currently called the principle of non-discrimination in trade. Samuel Crowther, whose work showed him to be a man of wide knowledge, experience and understanding, copyrighted in 1933 a book entitled "America Self-Contained". Chapter 9 of this book has the title "The free-trade myth." The chapter opens with a sentence which has the same meaning as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) gave a few minutes ago; it is this:
One of the most curious of the several classical economic delusions is that trade ever has been or ever can be free.
I say to hon. members, can you name any great nation of our time that became great through free trade? Has not every nation which became great used protection high enough to protect its industries until those industries became strong enough to compete with any industries in the world? Take Great Britain as an example. Britain is supposed to be a country that proves the soundness of free trade. I am not saying anything against free trade. I am putting some facts forward so that hon. members can read those facts and realize what almost fanatical delusions we see manifested by a great many inexperienced and uninformed Liberals who come into this house.
In Crowther's "America Self-Contained" there appear several statements bearing upon Britain and free trade. At page 165 we read:
The regulation of international trade by tariffs and other restrictions is now, and always has been, an affair of expediency, and what is today accepted as classical free-trade doctrine is only a record of what British industrialists considered best for Great Britain at a certain period of history.
You see that just simply shoots a hole right into the balloon of the free trade idealists. Speaking of Adam Smith, who is said to be the high priest of the free traders, Mr. Crowther says at page 165 of his book:
He did not advocate the repeal of protective duties in cases where an industry would be destroyed-
We can see how that applies to our beet sugar industry. Again, the author says:
-he put national defence above all other considerations.
Again, it is said:
He held that the navigation acts, which practically confined British trade to British ships, were necessary. . .

Again:
-he did not favour wiping out the British farmers by letting in free the products of virgin lands.
Let our free trade idealists weigh these facts. On page 166 we read this from Samuel Crowther:
Adam Smith did not bring free trade to England. It so happens that he wrote at a time when British industry was coming to the stage where it did not need protection from foreign industry so much as it needed entry into foreign markets.
In other words, British industries had become so strong that they could compete successfully with any other industries on the face of the earth. Mr. Crowther himself makes the following significant statement at page 169:
One might imagine that British trade had from the beginning been based on the free exchange of commodities. Nothing could be further from the facts. Up to the thirteenth century, England was a crude agricultural country supplying raw materials to the Hansards, who were known as the Easterlings, and since theirs was the only money in England, the name for their money, corrupted into "sterling", has survived. Edward III saw that the British wool might as well be woven at home, so he attracted a number of Flemish weavers and, as soon as they were well under way, prohibited the wearing of any articles made of foreign cloth. Some years later, foreign merchants were compelled by edict to lay out in British goods the proceeds realized on any articles they imported.
What do you think about that for free trade? Free trade was not the policy that Britain applied when she was becoming great. Then at page 170 we read from Samuel Crowther again:
The navigation act was the rock on which British trade was built.
That is significant, is it not? In other words the free trade policy of Great Britain, without the navigation act, even when Britain was using "free trade", would certainly not have sustained Britain in the great role which she played.
From page 177 in Samuel Crowther's book we read this passage:
There was really no freedom about British free trade. It was an entirely one-sided arrangement, for no country could sell manufactured goods in Britain at a price to compete with home-made articles, while of course England had no need to raise a barrier against the incoming of raw materials for her factories. So free trade really meant that every country would admit British goods instead of attempting to make its own.
There is a catch there. There are a number of people in the house who have indicated absolutely fantastic and fanatical addiction to the idea of free trade.
Let me draw these additional facts to the attention of all those who think too strongly about free trade. Britain was at that time the world's banker. Britain was also the 68108-1181
Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement world's insurance headquarters. Foreign competition with British goods had not grown up from Germany, the United States and from home industries such as we now find in Canada. Trade unionism had not yet developed in Britain. It was therefore possible for employers in Britain to force down labour to almost starvation levels.
These were the elements in Britain which enabled so-called free trade to work. Does anyone, even in the wildest nightmare, imagine that Canada could possibly get into a position similar to the one Britain occupied in those days? If Canada cannot get into the position in which Britain was at that time, how in the world can anyone sanely suggest that free trade for Canada would be sound?
I hope that my good friend the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), who is not in the chamber at the present moment, will give careful thought to these facts. Yet I sympathize with the statements he makes here concerning ultra high prices which result from too much tariff protection. We can go too far in the matter of tariff protection, and in many cases we have done so in Canada.
What about Germany? Did Germany become great because of free trade? Nothing of the sort. Friedrich List, a great thinker in the days of Bismarck, was invited by Bismarck to advise him as to how to build a great and powerful Germany, that Germany which we today dread in production and international competition. What did List advise? The most careful, elaborate and effective system of protection of German industries until they became powerful enough to compete successfully with industry anywhere on the face of the earth; and Germany was labouring under the disadvantage that the resources which she possessed were relatively exceedingly meagre for the population she had. She had to build herself out of woefully inadequate materials, but look what she did.
Now let us consider the United States. Upon what policies has she become great? Free trade? Not at all. Everybody knows how rigidly the United States has excluded goods from abroad. She was advised by this same Friedrich List who by the way was driven from Germany by certain people who did not like his ideas. He took refuge in the United States and taught the United States people the secrets of building their nation. So they built themselves into a nation which today, like a Colossus, bestrides the world. On free trade? No, not on free trade. We had therefore better be careful. I am not saying a word against free trade. I am merely putting on the record some facts

Canada-Cuba Sugar Agreement to which I hope the people in the country, particularly those in this house, will give a great deal of attention.
Then what about Canada? Canada has grown great relatively. What has she done it on? The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) gave several items which are protected quite generously by tariffs in Canada. I will just read a few of those for the benefit of people like the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing), who seem to imagine that any kind of protection is pernicious. We have asparagus protected by a tariff of 10 per cent; beans, green, 10 per cent; cabbage, 10 per cent; carrots and beets, 30 per cent; celery, 10 per cent; apples, 20 per cent-some of that has been removed; that was in 1947-sugar beets, 30 per cent; potatoes, 75 cents a hundred pounds; onions, 30 per cent; oats, 16 cents a bushel; rye, 15 cents a bushel; wheat, 30 cents a bushel; seeds, garden, 35 per cent.
How much of it is seasonal?
A good deal of it is seasonal and a good deal of it is not. For example, as to potatoes, it is not seasonal trade.
Oh, yes.

Potatoes? I will go right to the record with my hon. friend. I have It right here. Possibly he realizes that I know something about what is in that record. I have here on my desk the Canada Customs Tariff with amendments to June 1, 1950, so it is up to date; I think my hon. friend will agree with that. I can give him the pages on which those things are listed. For example, he will find potatoes on page 119, 75 cents a hundred pounds. I proceed with my list: whisky, $10 a gallon; soya beans, free; eggs. 10 cents a dozen; butter, 14 -cents; horses, $25; canned beef, 35 per cent; and so on down a long list that I do not think I will go through. But we have coal, including screenings and coal dust, protected by 75 cents. Let no one run away with the idea that Canada is a free trade country or has attained through free trade policies the degree of industrial development which she has attained. Let us not apply the doctrine, the dogma and the myth of free trade against the beet sugar industry because its advocates are seeking enough protection to enable it to grow as it should.
Others who are unsympathetic with the beet sugar industry contend that it is not efficient. I dare venture the opinion that if we could find an adequate score card by which to judge efficiency, it would be found that the beet sugar industry is probably one of the most efficient industries in the

Dominion of Canada. What do these people mean by "efficient" when they talk about "efficient"? As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said, I challenge any hon. member in the house or any person in the country to show that Canada is able to produce any commodity more cheaply than that commodity is being produced and sold somewhere else in the world. In other words, if we were to take away all protection from Canada, we soon would be using food and goods coming from everywhere on the face of the earth and we would not have anything produced with which to pay for them. That is precisely what we would face.
Now may I read a statement which I believe has a tremendous bearing on this whole matter of protection for the beet sugar industry. Here is a statement from a little publication called "Sugar Facts" dated February 3, 1953. It is headed "Cuba Sets Wage Rates". It states:
The government of Cuba, following meetings over the week-end, between the minister of labour and workers' representatives had announced its intention of fixing wages and salaries in the sugar industry at levels geared to a raw sugar price of $4.70 per 100 pounds f.o.b., 26 cents below the 1952 level of $4.96.
I ask you, what industry on the face of the earth could compete successfully with a country that is in a position to work together like that, so they can reduce their costs of production to the point where they can come in and compete successfully in the market of any country to which they desire to go. I am afraid that is exactly what we are facing in Cuba.
I greatly appreciate what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said to us today about the co-operative attitude of Cuba. If they decide to enter the Canadian market, they are able to do it. We do not have protection adequate to keep them out. I think the quota, possibly, is the best means of shielding our beet sugar industry. That is the means used in the United States. Some of these days perhaps I shall discuss the sugar quota as it is being employed in the sugar industry in the United States.
The beet sugar industry is of top-flight importance in respect of every one of the basic principles on which a nation is built enduring and strong. Without the beet sugar industry Canada cannot possibly attain selfsufficiency. Let me draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that today the United States is almost self-sufficient, and it is because of the fact that it is almost impossible to get United States dollars. If we want to be strong like the United States, what should our national aim be? Naturally, using

the United States as a model to govern ourselves by, it should be national self-sufficiency. And we cannot attain that without the Canadian beet sugar industry.
Without the beet sugar industry a genuinely balanced economy would be almost impossible to develop, if not utterly impossible. I am referring to an economy in which the primary producers, the farmers, could buy the products of the nation's industries. Without the beet sugar industry it will be extremely impracticable to maintain or to restore the richness of Canadian soils. No other industry I know of in Canada can be put to work and improve the soil while it produces a crop. Without the beet sugar industry it will be far more difficult to give employment to many Canadians, thus holding them in Canada where we want them, not down in the United States, after we have paid money to educate them.
Without the beet sugar industry it will be far more likely that we shall run into adverse trade balances, especially with the United States, from whom, in the last analysis, we buy a great deal of our sugar which we do not produce in Canada.
Considering the importance of the beet sugar industry to the Canadian economy, and considering only that, we must conclude that the admission of Cuban refined sugar into the Canadian market was highly regrettable.
It may be argued that the Canadian refiners are getting too much. I do not know about that; but I would say this, that before the government took the risky procedure of permitting Cuban refined sugar to come into this country, they ought to have found out what the situation was. They should not have let the Cuban refined sugar come in first, and then found out afterwards. That is a pretty reckless way of governing.
I maintain that the sooner we shut out Cuban refined sugar entirely, by a device similar to the one used in 1932, or by devices such as those suggested by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie), the better off we shall be, because this country is capable of producing in the Palliser triangle probably twice the amount of sugar we require, thus making the Palliser triangle a steppingstone to greatness rather than, possibly, a millstone around our necks.
